title: Matter is made of particles
keyIdea: Everything is made of tiny particles. How they are arranged and how they move explains solids, liquids and gases.

kid: All matter is made of particles that are far too small to see. In a solid, the particles are packed tightly in a fixed pattern and can only vibrate. In a liquid, they are close together but can slide past each other. In a gas, they are far apart and move fast in all directions.
This explains what we see. A solid keeps its shape. A liquid takes the shape of its container. A gas spreads out to fill any space.
adult: The particle model explains properties we can see. Gases can be squashed because there is empty space between the particles. Solids and liquids hardly squash at all, because their particles are already touching.
Heating gives particles more energy, so they vibrate or move faster. That's why heating can melt a solid or boil a liquid. The particles themselves do not get bigger or melt.

familyTip: Fill a syringe (with no needle) with air, block the end with your finger and push. Then try it with water.

practice.prompt: In which state are the particles far apart and moving fast in all directions?
practice.hint: Which state spreads out to fill a room?
practice.explain: In a gas the particles are far apart and move quickly.

practice.prompt: A substance melts at {m} °C and boils at {b} °C. What state is it in at {t} °C?
choices: Liquid, because {t} °C is between its melting and boiling points
Solid, because {t} °C is below its boiling point
Gas, because {t} °C is above its melting point
practice.hint: Is {t} °C above the melting point? Is it below the boiling point?
practice.explain: {t} °C is above {m} °C (so it has melted) and below {b} °C (so it hasn't boiled). It is a liquid.

practice.prompt: Why can a gas be squashed but a solid can't?
choices: Gas particles have big spaces between them
practice.explain: There is space between gas particles to push them into. Solid particles are already touching.

practice.prompt: When ice melts, what happens to its particles?
choices: They gain energy and start to slide past each other
practice.explain: The particles gain energy and break out of their fixed pattern. They are still the same particles.

practice.prompt: A sealed syringe holds {v} cm³ of air. You push the plunger until the air takes up half the space. What is the new volume in cm³?
practice.explain: Half of {v} is {=v/2} cm³. The same particles are just pushed closer together.

pool.prompt: Oxygen melts at −218 °C and boils at −183 °C. What state is oxygen in at {t} °C?
pool.explain: {t} °C is far above oxygen's boiling point of −183 °C, so it is a gas.

pool.prompt: A metal melts at {m} °C. What state is it in at {t} °C?
pool.hint: Is it hot enough to melt?
pool.explain: {t} °C is below its melting point of {m} °C, so it is still solid.

pool.prompt: Which state keeps its own shape?
pool.hint: Which particles are fixed in place?
pool.explain: Solid particles are held in a fixed pattern, so a solid keeps its shape.

pool.prompt: A smell spreads across a room. Why?
choices: Gas particles move around and spread out
Smells are not made of particles
Only warm air can carry smells
pool.hint: Gas particles move in all directions.
pool.explain: The smell's gas particles move and mix with the air particles until they spread out.

pool.prompt: What is between the particles in a gas?
pool.hint: Air is itself made of particles.
pool.explain: Nothing: there is empty space. Air can't be between them, because air is made of particles too.

pool.prompt: Ice and liquid water are made of the same particles. What is different?
choices: How the particles are arranged and move
What the particles are made of
pool.explain: Only the arrangement and movement change; the particles are the same.

pool.prompt: When you heat a gas in a sealed box, its particles…
pool.explain: More energy means faster particles. They don't grow.

visual.caption: Heat and cool the water. Watch the particles' arrangement and speed.
